title: The Gopis Abandon Their Homes
story:
The moon came up full over Vrindavan, washing the eastern sky with a red like the crimson powder worn on festival days. The forest stood soft in that light, the Yamuna carried it in broken pieces on the water, and the air held the deep quiet warmth of an autumn night. Krishna, the young cowherd whose songs the village loved, looked out at the night and the forest, raised his flute, and began to play.

The song called no one by name. It did not beg or command; it only drew, low and sweet, the way a remembered tune draws a listener back to it. It crossed the fields and the lanes and the courtyards of the village, and the cowherd women of Vrindavan heard it, and their hearts went out to meet it. It was the sound they had been waiting for without knowing it, and it made the quiet of the evening feel like a promise.

One woman was milking, and she left the cow standing with the pail half full, without a look back. One was serving the evening meal, and she set the dish down while it was still warm and walked out. One had a child at her breast, and she put the child down and went. One was anointing herself for the night and stopped where she sat; one had kohl half applied to her eyes and left it there, one eye dark and the other bare. Each of them had been in the middle of something, and each of them left it unfinished. The evening's work lay where it had dropped, and the houses stood as though time had stopped inside them.

Husbands caught at their arms, and fathers and brothers called after them, and the hands of their own kin closed over their wrists. It made no difference. The flute went on, unhurried, and the voices behind them rose and fell and were lost under the music. The women went, heedless of everything, because the sound of the flute had taken them and would not let them go.

Some could not go at all. The door was watched, or the house had closed in around them, and no way out could be found. Those women shut their eyes where they stood, some of them before they had even reached the door. The ache of being apart from the one they loved had grown too strong to bear, and when they closed their eyes it burned itself out, and whatever else had been in them went with it. With their eyes shut they went to him, and they found him as surely as the women who had crossed the fields.

By the time the others reached him, the moon stood high over the Yamuna. Krishna saw them coming through the trees — the milkmaid with the pail half full, the one with kohl on a single eye, and those who had never left their courtyards at all but had come to him with their eyes closed. Behind them the village slept on, unaware of who had slipped away from it. Before them the Yamuna lay dark and slow under the moon.
reflection: What stays in the mind is the inventory of unfinished things, the milk half-milked and the eye half-painted. The gopis are not shown renouncing anything with ceremony; they simply drop what they are doing mid-task because the flute interrupted a normal evening and they answered it. The detail that some could not leave at all, and still reached him by closing their eyes, quietly widens the story: the going is outward, but the meeting is not limited by walls.
next_story_tease: But the night was far from over; the dance had not yet begun.
hero_scene: Krishna standing in moonlight playing his flute by the Yamuna, while gopis hurry toward him across dark fields, one still carrying a half-filled milk pail, another with kohl on only one eye.
